black hole: A region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.
event horizon: The boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can return.
singularity: A point in a black hole where density and gravity become infinite and known physics breaks down.
machine learning: A field of computer science that gives computers the ability to learn from data without being explicitly programmed.
artificial intelligence: Artificial Intelligence (AI) — systems or machines that mimic human intelligence to perform tasks.
crispr: A genome-editing tool that can precisely modify DNA sequences in organisms.
photosynthesis: The process by which plants convert light energy into chemical energy (glucose) using CO2 and water.
acceleration: The rate of change of an object's velocity over time.
gravitational time dilation: A relativistic effect where time runs slower in stronger gravitational fields compared to weaker ones.
spaghettification: The extreme stretching effect objects experience when falling into a black hole due to tidal forces.
chemical reaction: A process in which one or more substances change into new substances with a different chemical makeup.
electrons: Tiny, negatively charged particles that surround the nucleus of an atom and are shared or transferred when atoms bond.
ionic bond: A chemical bond formed when one atom gives electrons to another, leaving two oppositely charged ions that attract each other.
covalent bonds: Chemical bonds formed when two atoms share pairs of electrons, usually between nonmetals.
endothermic: Describes a reaction that absorbs more energy from its surroundings than it releases.
exothermic: Describes a reaction that releases more energy, usually as heat, than it absorbs.
activation energy: The minimum amount of energy needed to get a chemical reaction started.
chemical equilibrium: The point in a reversible reaction where the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.
equilibrium constant: A number (K) that compares the amounts of products to reactants once a reaction reaches equilibrium.
gravitational field: The region around an object with mass where its gravity pulls on other objects.
newton’s laws: Isaac Newton's laws of motion and gravity, which describe how objects move and how masses pull on each other.
ice giant: A giant planet, like Uranus or Neptune, made mostly of water, ammonia, and methane ices rather than the hydrogen and helium that make up Jupiter and Saturn.
celestial object: Any naturally occurring object in space, such as a star, planet, moon, or asteroid.
dwarf planet: A round object that orbits the Sun like a planet but has not cleared other objects out of its orbit, such as Pluto.
kuiper belt: A vast ring of icy objects and dwarf planets that orbits the Sun beyond Neptune.
autonomous vehicle: A vehicle that uses sensors, cameras, and AI software to drive itself without a human driver.
lidar: A sensing method that fires pulses of laser light and times their reflections to measure distances and build 3D maps.
ultrasonic: Describes sound waves with frequencies too high for humans to hear, above about 20,000 hertz.
echolocation: A way of sensing surroundings by making sounds and listening to how their echoes bounce back.
radio waves: A type of electromagnetic radiation with long wavelengths, used in radar, radio, and wireless communication.
fossil fuel: A fuel such as coal, oil, or natural gas that formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient plants and animals.
bacteria: Single-celled microorganisms without a nucleus that live almost everywhere, including in and on the human body.
bacteriophage: A virus that infects and multiplies only inside bacteria.
dna: Deoxyribonucleic acid, the molecule that carries the genetic instructions for how a living thing grows, functions, and reproduces.
genome: The complete set of genetic material (DNA) in an organism.
immune system: The body's network of cells, tissues, and organs that defends against germs and other invaders.
cas proteins: Proteins guided by CRISPR RNA that act like molecular scissors, cutting DNA at a specific spot.
embryo: An organism in its earliest stage of development, when it is a small, growing cluster of cells.
germline: The reproductive cells (eggs and sperm) whose DNA is passed down to future generations.
sickle cell disease: An inherited blood disorder in which red blood cells become stiff and sickle-shaped, blocking blood flow.
big bang: The event about 13.8 billion years ago when the universe began expanding from an extremely hot, dense state.
cosmic microwave background: The faint leftover glow of radiation from the early universe that still fills all of space today.
dark energy: A mysterious form of energy that makes up about 68% of the universe and causes its expansion to speed up.
big freeze: A possible end of the universe in which it expands forever, growing colder and darker until the stars burn out; also called heat death.
big crunch: A possible end of the universe in which gravity halts the expansion and pulls everything back into a single hot, dense point.
big rip: A possible end of the universe in which dark energy grows so strong that it tears apart galaxies, stars, and even atoms.
northern hemisphere: The half of Earth that lies north of the equator.
preen glands: Glands near a bird's tail that produce oil it spreads through its feathers to keep them waterproof.
crustaceans: Mostly water-dwelling animals with hard outer shells and jointed legs, such as crabs, shrimp, and krill.
invertebrates: Animals without a backbone, such as insects, worms, jellyfish, and crustaceans.
conservation status: A rating of how close a species is to going extinct, ranging from Least Concern to Extinct.
habitat: The natural home of a plant or animal, where it finds food, shelter, and mates.
climate change: Long-term shifts in Earth's temperatures and weather patterns, driven mainly by human activities such as burning fossil fuels.
active recall: A study method in which you practice pulling information out of your memory instead of just rereading it.
neuroscience: The scientific study of the brain and nervous system.
neurons: Nerve cells that send electrical and chemical signals through the brain and body; AI models borrow the name for their simple processing units.
long-term potentiation: The lasting strengthening of connections between neurons that fire together, thought to be a basis of learning and memory.
forgetting curve: A curve, first mapped by Hermann Ebbinghaus, showing how quickly memories fade over time without review.
neural pathways: Chains of connected neurons that carry signals from one part of the nervous system to another.
motor regions: Areas of the brain that plan and control the body's voluntary movements.
sensory pathways: Chains of nerve cells that carry information from the senses to the brain.
dementia: A group of brain conditions that cause a lasting decline in memory, thinking, and everyday abilities.
binaural beats: An auditory illusion in which two slightly different tones played in each ear make the brain hear a third, pulsing beat.
piracetam: A memory drug prescribed in some countries but not approved by the FDA, often marketed online as a so-called smart drug.
industrial engineering: A branch of engineering that designs more efficient systems by organizing people, equipment, materials, and space.
fossils: Preserved remains or traces of ancient living things, such as bones, teeth, shells, or footprints, usually found in rock.
extinction: The permanent disappearance of a species once its last member has died.
southern hemisphere: The half of Earth that lies south of the equator.
ocean currents: Continuous, directed flows of seawater driven by wind, temperature, saltiness, and Earth's rotation.
habit formation: The process by which a behavior becomes automatic through repetition, often triggered by the same cue or setting.
genetics: The study of genes and how traits are passed down from parents to their offspring.
deindividualisation: A loss of self-awareness and personal identity that can happen in groups, making people more likely to act against their usual values.
conformity: Changing your beliefs or behavior to match those of a group.
cognitive dissonance: The mental discomfort felt when holding two conflicting beliefs, or when your actions go against your beliefs.
identical twins: Twins that develop from a single fertilized egg that splits in two, so they share nearly identical DNA.
criminology: The scientific study of crime, its causes, and how society responds to it.
plateau: A flat, raised area of land that rises sharply above the surrounding area on at least one side.
fossilization: The process by which the remains of ancient living things are preserved in rock over millions of years.
hydrocarbon: A compound made only of hydrogen and carbon atoms; hydrocarbons are the main ingredients of fossil fuels.
molecules: Groups of two or more atoms held together by chemical bonds.
glaciers: Huge masses of ice, built up from compacted snow, that slowly flow under their own weight.
ice age: A long period when Earth's climate is cold enough for ice sheets and glaciers to cover large areas of land.
limestone: A sedimentary rock made mostly of calcium carbonate, often from ancient shells, that slowly dissolves in acidic water.
iron ore: Rock containing iron compounds that can be mined and refined to make iron and steel.
tectonic plates: Giant slabs of Earth's outer shell that slowly move, causing earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain building.
chloroplast: A structure inside plant cells that captures sunlight and carries out photosynthesis.
thylakoid: A flattened, disk-shaped sac inside a chloroplast whose membrane holds chlorophyll and carries out the light-dependent reactions.
stroma: The fluid-filled space inside a chloroplast that surrounds the thylakoids, where the Calvin cycle takes place.
chlorophyll: The green pigment in plants that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
electron transport chain: A series of proteins in a membrane that pass electrons along, using their energy to pump hydrogen ions across the membrane.
photosystem: A cluster of proteins and pigments that absorbs light and uses its energy to excite electrons.
atp: Adenosine triphosphate, the molecule cells use as their main short-term energy carrier.
nadph: An energy-rich molecule that carries electrons from the light-dependent reactions to the Calvin cycle.
calvin cycle: The light-independent stage of photosynthesis, where carbon dioxide is built into sugar using energy from ATP and NADPH.
limbic system: A set of brain structures involved in emotions, motivation, and memory.
prefrontal cortex: The front part of the brain responsible for planning, decision-making, and self-control.
adhd: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, a condition that affects attention, impulse control, and activity level.
greenhouse gas: A gas, such as carbon dioxide or methane, that traps heat in Earth's atmosphere and contributes to global warming.
decarbonize: To reduce or eliminate the carbon dioxide emissions produced by an activity, company, or economy.
primate: A member of the group of mammals that includes lemurs, monkeys, apes, and humans.
adaptations: Inherited traits that help an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
isotopic analysis: A lab technique that measures the different forms (isotopes) of elements in teeth or bones to reveal what an animal ate and where it lived.
enamel: The hard, mineral-rich outer layer of a tooth.
neural networks: Networks of connected neurons; in AI, computer systems built from layers of artificial neurons, loosely modeled on the brain, that learn patterns from data.
algorithms: Step-by-step sets of instructions that a computer follows to solve a problem or complete a task.
base pairs: Matching pairs of chemical units in DNA (A with T, and C with G) that form the rungs of its twisted ladder.
polygenic risk scores: Estimates of a person's chance of developing a disease based on the combined effects of many small genetic differences.
metagenomics: The study of all the genetic material from a whole community of microbes, such as the bacteria living in the gut.
epigenetic: Describes chemical changes that switch genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence itself.
methylation: The attachment of small chemical tags called methyl groups to DNA, which can switch genes off.
deep learning: A type of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers to learn complex patterns from large amounts of data.
input layer: The first layer of a neural network, which receives the raw data.
hidden layers: The layers of a neural network between the input and output layers, where most of the pattern-finding happens.
output layer: The final layer of a neural network, which produces the model's prediction or answer.
facial recognition: Technology that identifies or verifies a person by analyzing the features of their face.
olfactory receptors: Proteins on nerve cells in the nose that detect odor molecules and send smell signals to the brain.
nasal cavity: The air-filled space inside the nose, behind the nostrils.
vomeronasal organ: A smell organ inside the nasal cavity of many animals that detects pheromones.
pheromones: Chemical signals released by an animal that affect the behavior of other members of its species.
nutrients: Substances in food, such as proteins, vitamins, and minerals, that living things need to grow and stay healthy.
hair follicles: Tiny tube-shaped structures in the skin that produce and anchor each hair.
hair bulb: The rounded base of a hair, deep inside the follicle, where new hair cells are made.
nervous system: The body's network of the brain, spinal cord, and nerves that carries signals to control what the body does.
epilepsy: A brain disorder in which bursts of abnormal electrical activity cause repeated seizures.
hemispherectomy: A surgery that removes or disconnects one half (hemisphere) of the brain to stop severe seizures.
neurosurgery: Surgery on the brain, spinal cord, or nerves.
cerebrospinal fluid: The clear fluid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord.
neuroplasticity: The brain's ability to rewire itself by forming new connections throughout life, especially after injury.
gills: Breathing organs that let fish and other water animals take in oxygen dissolved in water.
larva: An immature early form of an animal that looks very different from the adult, like a caterpillar or tadpole.
planula: The tiny, free-swimming larva of a jellyfish or other cnidarian.
polyps: The tube-shaped stage of animals like jellyfish and corals that attaches to a surface, with a mouth ringed by tentacles.
medusa: The free-swimming, bell-shaped adult stage of a jellyfish.
transdifferentiation: The process in which one type of specialized cell turns directly into a different type of specialized cell.
food chain: The order in which living things eat one another, passing energy from plants and algae up to top predators.
amphibians: Cold-blooded vertebrates, like frogs and salamanders, that usually start life in water and later can live on land.
regeneration: The ability of a living thing to regrow lost or damaged cells, tissues, or body parts.
blastema: A mass of cells that forms at a wound and can grow into the missing tissue or limb.
critically endangered: The highest risk category for a wild species, meaning it faces an extremely high risk of extinction.
genetic diversity: The variety of genes within a species, which helps populations adapt and survive.
introduced species: A species brought by humans to a place where it doesn't naturally live, often harming native wildlife.
drag: A force that pushes against an object moving through air or water, slowing it down.
air pressure: The force that air molecules exert as they push against surfaces.
downforce: A downward force created by air flowing over a car's wings and body, pressing it onto the track for more grip.
traction: The grip between a tire and the road that keeps it from slipping.
centrifugal force: The apparent outward pull felt by an object moving along a curved path.
friction: A force that resists two surfaces sliding against each other.
aerodynamics: The study of how air flows around objects, like cars and planes, and the forces it creates.
wind tunnel: A tunnel where air is blown over a vehicle or model so engineers can study how the air flows around it.
cnidarian: A member of a group of simple water animals with stinging cells, including jellyfish, corals, sea anemones, and hydras.
stem cells: Unspecialized cells that can divide and develop into many different types of cells.
nematocysts: Tiny stinging capsules in the tentacles of cnidarians that fire a harpoon-like thread to catch prey.
nerve net: A simple web of nerve cells spread throughout the body of brainless animals like jellyfish and hydras.
algae: Simple, plant-like organisms, mostly living in water, that make their own food through photosynthesis.
budding: A form of asexual reproduction in which a new organism grows out of the parent's body and then breaks off.
alpine: Describes high mountain areas above the tree line, with cold temperatures, strong winds, and thin air.
lichen: An organism made of a fungus living in partnership with algae or bacteria, often growing on rocks and trees.
conifer: A tree, such as a pine or fir, that produces cones and usually has needle-shaped leaves.
respiratory systems: The organs, including the lungs and airways, that take in oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.
sinkhole: A hole or depression in the ground that forms when the surface collapses into an empty space underground.
soluble: Able to dissolve in a liquid, such as water.
groundwater: Water that fills the cracks and spaces in soil and rock beneath Earth's surface.
water table: The underground level below which the soil and rock are completely soaked with water.
cenotes: Natural sinkholes, common in Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, that expose pools of groundwater.
psychosocial development: How a person's personality and sense of self grow through social relationships and experiences across their life.
psychoanalysis: A theory and type of therapy, founded by Sigmund Freud, that explores how unconscious thoughts and feelings shape behavior.
identity crisis: A period of uncertainty and confusion about who you are and what role you play in society.
sociocultural theory: Lev Vygotsky's theory that people learn and develop through social interaction and the culture around them.
genetic engineering: Directly changing an organism's DNA to give it new traits.
cloning: Creating a living thing that is a genetically identical copy of another.
vaccine: A substance that trains the immune system to recognize and fight a specific germ without causing the disease.
pandemic: An outbreak of disease that spreads across many countries or the whole world.
covid-19: The disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, which sparked a global pandemic beginning in 2020.
ice shelf: A thick, floating sheet of ice attached to a coastline, formed where glaciers flow out onto the sea.
global warming: The long-term rise in Earth's average temperature, mainly caused by greenhouse gases from human activities.
hydrogen bonds: Weak attractions between a hydrogen atom in one molecule and an oxygen or nitrogen atom in a nearby molecule.
phytoplankton: Microscopic, plant-like organisms that drift in the ocean, make food from sunlight, and form the base of most marine food chains.
erosion: The wearing away and carrying off of rock and soil by water, wind, or ice.
ecosystems: Communities of living things interacting with each other and with their physical environment.
embryo twinning: A cloning method in which an early embryo is split into parts that each grow into genetically identical animals.
somatic cell nuclear transfer: A cloning method in which the nucleus of a body cell is placed into an egg cell whose own nucleus has been removed.
uterus: The organ in female mammals where a baby develops before birth; also called the womb.
egg cell: The female reproductive cell, which can develop into a new organism after fertilization.
cybersecurity: The practice of protecting computers, networks, and data from attacks and unauthorized access.
cyberattacks: Deliberate attempts to break into, damage, or steal from computers or networks.
deepfakes: Fake videos, images, or audio made with AI that realistically show people saying or doing things they never did.
wormholes: Theoretical tunnels through spacetime that could connect two distant points in the universe.
accretion disk: A swirling disk of hot gas and dust spiraling into a massive object like a black hole, glowing as it heats up.
schwarzschild metric: The solution to Einstein's equations that describes how spacetime curves around a round, non-spinning mass like a black hole.
geodesic: The shortest path between two points on a curved surface or through curved spacetime.
spacetime: The four-dimensional fabric that combines the three dimensions of space with time.
time dilation: The slowing of time for an object moving very fast or in strong gravity, compared to an outside observer.
general relativity: Einstein's theory that gravity is the bending of spacetime by mass and energy.
gravity assist: A spaceflight maneuver that uses a planet's gravity to change a spacecraft's speed and direction while saving fuel.
differential equation: An equation that relates a quantity to the rate at which it changes.
euler’s method: A step-by-step technique for approximating the solution of a differential equation by following small tangent-line steps.
